articles.text: The first shipment of tea direct from China, over the N. P. is now going on. One cargo will make two hundred car loads.
articles.summary: The first direct shipment of China tea over the Northern Pacific is under way, one cargo filling 200 car loads.

articles.text: The question of opening the Oklahoma country to settlement has been seriously considered by the cabinet and the last report seemed to indicate that it will soon be done.
articles.summary: The cabinet is reported near to opening the Oklahoma country to settlement.

articles.text: We willingly give Chicago every credit due her, but when the Inter Ocean cracks her up as a summer resort and talks about the pure air from the lake and prairies; fragrant memories of Bridgeport and Chicago river oblige us to put in an emphatic denial. As a summer resort Chicago is not a success.
articles.summary: Packard mocks the Chicago Inter Ocean's promotion of Chicago as a summer resort.

articles.text: The Montana stock association will assemble for its fall meeting at Helena, Aug. 26. The Little Missouri association should have a meeting before that time to report to the Helena meeting. There was no definite time set for our fall meeting but one should be set now. The constitution calls for two yearly meetings and it will undoubtedly be best to have ours before that of the Helena association. It is time for some of our officers to come to the front with a notice of the meeting.
articles.summary: With the Montana stock association meeting at Helena Aug. 26, the paper urges the Little Missouri association's officers to call a fall meeting first.

articles.text: The census report of northern Dakota will probably be finished to-morrow. Major Edwards has been hurrying the work as fast as was consistent with accuracy and our report is far in advance of that of southern Dakota. From reports, we judge that the enumeration will show a gratifying increase in all directions. In conjunction with that of southern Dakota, it will show that we are far better prepared to become a state in all that concerns material welfare than are at least a half dozen of the present states.
articles.summary: The northern Dakota census under Major Edwards is expected to be finished the next day and, the paper says, will strengthen the case for statehood.

articles.text: Our second and third pages give such a detailed account of the life and death of General Grant, that anything further is almost superfluous. We must, however, put in our mite to swell the volume of sentiment against the burial of the General in New York. Riverside park, an extension of Central park has now been selected as his last resting place. It is by no means appropriate that he should be buried in a pleasure ground. Washington is the only fit place to receive the remains of such a national character as was Grant.
articles.summary: Packard objects to General Grant's burial in Riverside Park, New York, arguing Washington is the only fit place.

articles.text: The cattlemen of the Cheyenne and Arapahoe reservation in Indian Territory have gathered in force at Kansas City and unite in petitioning the president to extend the date of removal from forty days to one year. Reports are coming in that the Indians are already beginning to slaughter the cattle on the reservation and the cattlemen are positively at a standstill as to what to do. Further developments are anxiously awaited. It is by no means probable that the Executive will grant an extension until he finds that an honest effort will not remove the cattle in forty days.
articles.summary: Cheyenne and Arapahoe reservation cattlemen meeting at Kansas City petition the president to extend their forty-day removal order to a year.

articles.headline: ADDITIONAL LOCAL.
articles.text: The Hashknife herd to be delivered the 1st. has been grazing on the divide for several weeks. They are said to be in good condition.
articles.summary: The Hashknife herd due for delivery on the 1st has been grazing on the divide for weeks and is in good condition.

articles.text: Mrs. J. L. Truscott, nee Miss Maggie Gardient, arrived Monday evening. She will live at the Northern Pacific until Mr. Truscott finishes his house on the ranch.
articles.summary: Mrs. J. L. Truscott (nee Maggie Gardient) arrived Monday evening and will stay at the Northern Pacific hotel until her husband finishes their ranch house.

articles.text: The fast freights on the N. P. will not start until next Sunday. They will make the run from St. Paul to Portland in 160 hours and take the places of freights 13 and 16.
articles.summary: N. P. fast freights, running St. Paul to Portland in 160 hours, will start next Sunday, replacing freights 13 and 16.

articles.text: The sad news was received last Sunday that Janie Fitzgerald was dead. It will be a surprise to many of her acquaintances even to know that she was seriously ill. It was but a short time ago that she seemed full of life and health and to be cut down in her young womanhood seems scarcely possible.
articles.summary: News of the death of Janie Fitzgerald reached Medora last Sunday.

articles.text: J. L. DeHart, of the DeHart Land and Cattle Co., whose range is on the Rosebud passed through on his way east this morning. He reports that the grasshoppers are doing a great deal of damage on the Rosebud and vicinity. The reports of seventeen-year locusts appearing, at least in his district, are unfounded. Several firms in his vicinity will begin shipping beef in a week.
articles.summary: J. L. DeHart of the DeHart Land and Cattle Co. passed through and reported grasshopper damage on the Rosebud and beef shipping to start within a week.

articles.text: The dam recently built above the cut seemed to do little good Tuesday evening in turning the rush of water from the freight house. An immense quantity of rain seemed to have fallen several miles down the track and in its rush under the freight house it tore away the underpinning so that the building sagged over a foot in the middle. New propping has been put in, but the building will have to be raised.
articles.summary: Tuesday evening's flood water tore the underpinning from the Medora freight house, which sagged over a foot and will have to be raised.

articles.text: We have noticed several articles in our exchanges relative to the attacks of the "heel fly." Although the existence of such a fly seems to be credited by a number of cattlemen, we very much doubt its existence. We have never yet seen a responsible cowman who asserted that he had seen a "heel fly" and that the peculiar antics cut by cows at times is due to the attacks of the fly. The true explanation in all probability, is that the peculiar actions are caused by the working out of grubs on the animal for the results are exactly similar from this cause in districts where "heel flies" are never mentioned.
articles.summary: The paper doubts the existence of the 'heel fly' and blames grubs for cattle's odd antics.

articles.text: B. F. Reynolds arrived from Texas Monday and will make his head-quarters at Medora for a time. He has forty-five hundred Texas cattle on the trail, now in the neighborhood of Rapid City. Thirteen hundred of these cattle will be sold and the rest will probably be grazed in this vicinity. Mr. Reynolds cattle being from northern Texas, he had no difficulty in driving, from the quarantine laws. He reports the feeling between northern and southern Texas cowmen as being far more bitter than that between the former and northwestern cattlemen. He does not consider that there ever will be a permanent stop put to driving by trail. The discovery of the causes and cure of Texas fever will again send thousands of cattle from Texas to the north.
articles.summary: B. F. Reynolds arrived from Texas Monday to headquarter at Medora; his 4,500 Texas cattle on the trail are near Rapid City.

articles.text: The most interesting thing of late to cattlemen is the order of President Cleveland, warning cattlemen and "other intruders" to leave the Indian Territory within forty days. There are two very distinct sides to this question. On the one hand, the present residents and owners of cattle in the Indian Territory are for the most part innocent sub-lessees. The organized lessees are wealthy speculators who took the chances of their leases from the Indians being declared illegal, the Interior department merely giving them their tacit consent. Nevertheless, innocent parties will for the most part be sufferers unless they can make the original lessees responsible for all damage. On the other hand, if the government did not declare the leases illegal and compel cattlemen to remove, they would most certainly break faith with the Indians. Up to the present, no move has been made toward driving the cattle out and a policy of delay has been inaugurated which, in view of the present attitude of the administration, can only do harm to the cattle owners. But where in the world to drive between 400,000 and 500,000 head of cattle is what is bothering the Territory cowmen. Neither Kansas, Colorado or Nebraska can possibly find room for them and it is too late in the season to drive as far north as Dakota or Montana. If the cattlemen take immediate steps to try and carry out the executive order the limit of forty days can easily be extended. If the present dilatory policy is kept up, it can but result in immense loss to the cattlemen. The COW BOY has too often declared its sentiments on the reservation question to be misunderstood. We believe thoroughly that every Indian reservation should be thrown open to settlement except say 160 acres for each Indian and an honest manner of conducting the distribution of food to the Indians be inaugurated. This is the only way to settle the difficulty and the way it must finally be decided.
articles.summary: Editorial on President Cleveland's order removing cattlemen from Indian Territory, urging compliance and restating the paper's view that reservations should be opened to settlement.

articles.summary: Cigar drummer Abe Goodkind called on Medora dealers Tuesday.

articles.summary: Pat O'Hara sold his house in Little Missouri, formerly occupied by Mrs. Lason.

articles.text: T. A. Matthews, formerly foreman for the N. P. R. C. Co., has been appointed inspector of the Montana stock association, to be stationed at St. Paul.
articles.summary: T. A. Matthews, former N. P. Refrigerator Car Co. foreman, was appointed Montana stock association inspector at St. Paul.

articles.text: Prices on all classes of cattle dropped fifteen to twenty-five cents in the Chicago market during the last week, as will be seen by our market report.
articles.summary: Chicago cattle prices fell 15 to 25 cents during the week.

articles.text: Rattlesnakes are more abundant this year than for a long time in the Bad Lands. From the number now being killed it is to be hoped that we will soon be rid of them.
articles.summary: Rattlesnakes are unusually abundant in the Bad Lands this year.

articles.text: Never, since the first white man came here, has there been as much rain as we have had this season. There has even been more than is wanted as the grass should at this time be better cured than it is.
articles.summary: The season has been the wettest since white settlement, leaving the grass poorly cured.

articles.text: No service was held last Sunday evening, although Rev. Schaffner was here, owing to the improvements going on in the rink. Next Sunday evening service will be held in the depot waiting room, where all are invited.
articles.summary: No service was held last Sunday because of work on the rink; next Sunday's service will be in the depot waiting room.

articles.text: Strange as it may seem, Medora has a larger freight, express and passenger business than any point on the division, Mandan and Glendive included. Fifteen to twenty thousand dollars is no uncommon freight business to do in a month.
articles.summary: Medora does more freight, express and passenger business than any point on its N. P. division.

articles.text: Max Bass has "struck his gait" as agent for the Milwaukee Brewing Co. It must needs be a temperance town where his persuasive eloquence will not introduce the now famous Bismarck beer. The brewing company would have had a hard time finding a better man to compete with "Otto, the spotter." We live in hopes of seeing the two in town together. There will certainly be room for an argument then.
articles.summary: Max Bass is now agent for the Milwaukee Brewing Co., selling Bismarck beer.

articles.text: D. F. Barry, "Bismarck's best" in the photograph line, has placed us under many obligations for a number of large panels and photographs of noted Indians, Sitting Bull, Rain-in-the-Face, Slow White Buffalo, Crow Eagle, Iron Thunder, Fool Thunder, Standing Holy, Sitting Bull's daughter, Gaul and nephew and others all bedecked in Indian finery are among the number. Mr. Barry has made a specialty of Indian photographs, he having a gallery at Standing Rock. He is thinking of putting up a gallery here and taking a number of Bad Lands views.
articles.summary: Bismarck photographer D. F. Barry gave the Cow Boy photographs of Sitting Bull and other noted Indians and may open a gallery at Medora.

articles.text: The St. Paul jobbers came in like a cloud of seventeen-year locusts but apparently with no such greedy design. Their trip is one, more of pleasure than business, but a weather eye was always kept open for trade. The excursion train arrived at 4:30 and immediately the Northwestern band enlivened all with the first strains of brass-band music that have ever been heard in Medora. The whole party then fell in and headed by the band marched to the slaughter-house. Here the busy scene was viewed for a few minutes and the system displayed was warmly approved. On the return trip considerable amusement was aroused by Pete the cook, who was riding a kicking cayuse and passing as chief of police. The only real, live, wild, genuine, untamed cow-puncher, disporting on his native heath was Fred Willard. To look at his calm, untroubled lineaments while stating to an eager questioner that his revolver cost two hundred and sixty dollars and other answers of a like tenor, one would actually have believed what he said—if he didn't know him. The excursionists expressed themselves as especially sorry not to be able to stop and learn something of the cattle business, but this, of course was impossible. The trip will last ten days from the time of starting, the western limit being Butte. The trip will give the jobbers a good idea of the growth of the country along the line as well as its needs. The trip cannot but be mutually profitable as this whole country naturally claims St. Paul as a headquarters.
articles.summary: An excursion train of St. Paul jobbers stopped at Medora with the Northwestern band, the first brass band heard there, and marched to the slaughter-house.

articles.text: The "Dude" seems still to be at his funny work. Some one had better cork him up.
articles.summary: A jab at a local joker known as the "Dude."

articles.text: Jack Bullion came in yesterday from his ranch and reported that between his ranch on Bullion creek and Van Eeghan's on Garner creek a heavy hail storm occurred last Saturday. In some places the hail was piled up a foot deep. There was only a narrow strip in which the hail fell and no damage was done.

articles.text: Tuesday, owing to the absence of wind was the most oppressive day the inhabitants of Medora have ever experienced. Until half past two the sun itself fairly sweltered. Then a rain storm accompanied by hail set in and in half an hour lowered the temperature to seventy-one, a decrease of twenty-nine degrees.
articles.summary: Tuesday was Medora's most oppressive day until a hail and rain storm dropped the temperature 29 degrees in half an hour.

articles.text: W. T. Ingersoll, the best photographer in St. Paul went through Medora with the St. Paul jobbers, on his way to the National Park. He will remain there about five weeks and on his return will stop off at Medora provided enough work is guaranteed him to pay expenses. He will then take a number of views of the Bad Lands which our citizens and others are anxious to secure.
articles.summary: St. Paul photographer W. T. Ingersoll passed through with the jobbers en route to Yellowstone and may return to photograph the Bad Lands.

articles.text: Ed. Drury, deputy-sheriff of Morton Co., came up Monday evening and served an attachment on the Cantonment property. The attachment was issued at the instance of Bellows & Co., of Mandan. It is difficult to determine the effect of Commodore Gorringe's death on this property, especially as the original title to the property is in dispute. The matter will probably be straightened out at the coming term of court in Morton county.
articles.summary: Morton County deputy sheriff Ed. Drury served an attachment on the Cantonment property for Bellows & Co. of Mandan; Commodore Gorringe's death complicates the disputed title.

articles.headline: The Horoscope Fiend.
articles.text:
"Do you want a horoscope, I don't know."

The above was addressed to William, he of cold turkey fame. William, seated behind his dry-goods counter and being in the midst of a calculation as to how many cold turkeys at steen bits a piece it would take to satisfy the yearnings of an empty stomach such as his; said "naw."

The mouth and head from which had emanated the opening sentence was slowly withdrawing when William had a sudden thought and yelled: "Say, is them hoorahscopes good to eat."

The head popped suddenly forward, followed by a body and a pair of bandy legs and the same voice said: "No, my christian friend, they are not fit for the feast unless viewed from an allegorical or intellectual standpoint. Viewed thus they beat the mental pabulum of the immortal gods. A horoscope, my dear friend is a fortune-telling instrument that tells your lucky star and through this, your subsequent fortunes and misfortunes. What was your birthday?"

On being informed that it was the thirtieth of February, the horoscope fiend said:

"You were born under a lucky star. You will become wealthy and fat. You delight in hard work and love good things to eat. You must never gamble with your face toward the east. Always think of something pleasant, to eat for instance, when throwing dice and you will always be lucky."

"Well" said William, let's test this thing. I will face the east and bet you $5 I beat you a game of seven up."

This the horoscopist declined as also several other invitations of like nature, besides hints to the effect that talking was dry work.

Some of the boys meantime had been rigging up a pail of water over the door which accidentally fell on him as he started out after tripping flat on an invisible wire that had carelessly been stretched at just the right distance to have such an effect.

Monday the boys were going to have him up on a charge of heresy before Judge Gordon, but he had left the winsome Bad Lands far behind and was probably by that time working the inhabitants of Glendive.
articles.summary: Humorous account of an itinerant horoscope seller's encounter with storekeeper William and a prank by 'the boys' before he left for Glendive.
